# The Phantasia-Orexis-Kinesis Circuit: Aristotle on Imagination, Desire, and Animal Movement 

## 1. Aristotle, Phantasia, and Imagination (φαντασία) The investigation of animal movement in Aristotle's corpus requires, at its foundation, a careful elaboration of the faculty of phantasia—a term that, as Christina Papachristou observes, resists straightforward translation into the English "imagination" and is perhaps better left untranslated so as to preserve its distinctive Aristotelian resonance (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). Indeed, the very decision to render φαντασία as "imagination" risks importing modern connotations of creative fancy that are largely alien to Aristotle's account, which is rooted not in productive invention but in the residual movement generated by actual sense-perception; accordingly, we shall proceed with due caution, attending closely to the primary text and its internal distinctions. At the most fundamental level, Aristotle situates phantasia as a capacity that arises from and depends upon αἴσθησις, perception, yet is not reducible to it: phantasia is that faculty through which an image or φάντασμα persists and can be entertained even after the sensible object has withdrawn from the perceptual field. It is thus a movement resulting from actual sensation, one that enables the living being to sustain cognitive and motivational contact with its environment beyond the immediate moment of perceptual encounter (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 36). The distinction between sensitive phantasia and deliberative phantasia constitutes one of the most consequential internal differentiations within Aristotle's psychology. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in De Anima III.11, "Sensitive imagination, as we have said, is found in all animals, deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). This passage is of considerable importance for several reasons: it establishes that all animals, insofar as they possess perception, are endowed with sensitive phantasia and hence with the minimal capacity to retain and be moved by phantasmata; and it simultaneously reserves deliberative phantasia for those beings—principally human beings—who are capable of calculation and rational comparison. The calculative dimension of deliberative phantasia involves measuring competing ends against a single standard, thereby introducing the possibility of practical reasoning into the motivational circuit. Papachristou's analysis underscores the significance of this gradation; the division into kinds or grades of phantasia within De Anima is not merely classificatory but reflects genuine differences in the complexity of animal life and its relation to action (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 6–7). Furthermore, the relationship between phantasia and belief (δόξα) deserves attention, for Aristotle is careful to distinguish the two: phantasia can present what is false without the accompanying commitment or assent characteristic of belief, and it is in this respect voluntary in a manner that doxa is not. The user is able, as it were, to summon up images at will, whereas belief is constrained by evidence and rational persuasion. This voluntariness of phantasia is critical to understanding how it functions within the practical circuit, for it means that the animal's orientation toward its environment is shaped not merely by what is given in sensation but by how the sensible content is organized, selected, and interpreted through phantasmata. As the bridge between Nussbaum and Aristotle suggests, to move a creature to action, an object must appear to it through selection, marking off, organization, and interpretation—a process that is precisely the work of phantasia. Aristotle himself insists that even so basic a function as voice production requires the accompaniment of this faculty: "what produces the impact must have soul in it and must be accompanied by an act of imagination, for voice is a sound with a meaning" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 32). Thus phantasia is not an ornamental addition to animal psychology but a necessary condition for meaningful engagement with the world, mediating between bare sensory reception and the motivated, purposive movement that characterizes animal life. The tension between phantasia's causal derivation from sensation and its functional autonomy in domains such as dreaming, deliberation, and involuntary movement will be addressed more fully in subsequent chapters; here it suffices this tension is productively unresolved in Aristotle's corpus and constitutes one of the central puzzles of his philosophical psychology. 

## 2. Aristotle, Orexis, and Desire (ὄρεξις) If phantasia furnishes the cognitive content—the φάντασμα—that structures the animal's apprehension of its environment, it is ὄρεξις, desire or appetition, that supplies the motive force without which the phantasma would remain inert and motivationally impotent. Aristotle's account of animal movement in De Anima III.9–11 is emphatic on this point: neither phantasia alone nor thought alone is sufficient to initiate movement; rather, it is desire, oriented toward something that appears good or pleasant through the work of phantasia, that constitutes the immediate efficient cause of locomotion. The totality of involvements through which the animal is enmeshed in its world thus depends upon the conjunction of phantasia and orexis—the former presenting the object under a certain description, the latter reaching toward it as something to be pursued or fled. Accordingly, the practical circuit described in De Anima III.10 takes the form of a syllogism-like structure in which a general desire provides the major premiss, a phantasia-mediated perception of the particular situation provides the minor premiss, and the conclusion is the action itself (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). This account of desire is given considerable phenomenological specificity in the *Rhetoric*, where Aristotle attends to the affective dimensions of ὄρεξις—to the ways in which desire, fear, anger, and other πάθη condition the agent's orientation toward objects and courses of action. The narration of character in rhetorical discourse, Aristotle suggests, is achieved precisely through the indication of choice, for "the quality of purpose indicated determines the quality of character depicted and is itself determined by the end pursued" (Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, p. 114). This passage is illuminating for our purposes because it reveals that desire, as the faculty oriented toward ends, is the locus of characterological determination: what an agent desires reveals what kind of being it is. Similarly, Aristotle's discussion of practicable goods in the *Rhetoric* emphasizes that "things easily effected" are those "in which everyone, or most people, or one's equals, or one's inferiors have succeeded" (Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, p. 18), thereby connecting the structure of desire to the perceived accessibility and magnitude of its objects. The desirable is not merely what is good in itself but what appears attainable and proportionate—an appearance that is, once again, furnished by phantasia. Heidegger's interpretation is instructive here, for he draws attention to the way in which πάθη—the affections or dispositions that accompany and partly constitute desire—are not mere subjective states but modes of being-in-the-world. (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), "These πάθη, 'affects,' are not states pertaining to ensouled things, but are concerned with a disposition of living things in their world, in the mode of being positioned toward something, allowing a matter to matter to it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 96–98). This reading recasts orexis and its associated affects as fundamentally relational and world-disclosing: desire is not a blind impulse enclosed within the animal's body but a reaching-toward that opens up the environment as a field of significance. Hence the convergence of phantasia and orexis is not merely a causal mechanism but a structure of disclosure—it is through phantasia-informed desire that the animal's world becomes a totality of involvements laden with practical import. Moreover, the corporeal dimension of orexis is underscored in De Motu Animalium, where (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) "Blind courage and panic fears, erotic motions, and the rest of the corporeal affections, pleasant and painful, are all accompanied by heating or chilling, some in a particular member, others in the body generally" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, pp. 8–9). The somatic mediation of desire—its expression through changes in bodily temperature, heartbeat, and muscular readiness—ensures that orexis is never purely psychic but always already embodied, bridging the gap between the soul's intentional orientation and the body's capacity for movement. 

## 3. Aristotle opens his investigation of animal movement in De Motu Animalium by acknowledging that while specific kinds of locomotion have been treated elsewhere, "there remains an investigation of the common cause of any sort of animal movement whatsoever" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 1). This search for a common cause is precisely what leads Aristotle to the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit, for the universal structure underlying all varieties of animal locomotion is not mechanical but psychological: it is the conjunction of cognitive appearance and appetitive orientation that constitutes the ἀρχή, the origin, of movement in every case. The practical syllogism formalizes this structure by compressing a general desire, a phantasia-mediated perception of particular circumstances, and the resulting action into a single inferential sequence; subsequently, the action follows the perception of the particular with a kind of necessity analogous to the logical necessity of a conclusion drawn from premisses. Aristotle is explicit that thinking and imagination produce the forms that bring about the bodily affections involved in movement: "For thinking and imagination, as we said above, produce that which brings about the affections, since they produce the forms which bring them about" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). This passage is crucial because it specifies the mechanism by which the psychic faculties of phantasia and νοῦς exercise causal efficacy upon the body: they produce the forms—the εἴδη—that in turn bring about the physiological changes (heating, chilling, expansion, contraction) that constitute the proximate material cause of locomotion. The parts thus affected "display this motion more conspicuously than the rest, because each is in a sense a separate animal, the reason being that each contains vital moisture" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). Hence the bridge between psychic form and bodily motion is mediated by the vital moisture (σύμφυτον πνεῦμα) that renders the bodily parts responsive to the forms produced by phantasia and thought. Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's concept of κίνησις deepens this analysis by situating movement within a broader ontological framework. In his account, κίνησις is not merely spatial displacement but the actuality of the potential qua potential—a determination of being that pervades the entirety of Aristotle's physics and metaphysics. (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) "the being-context about which I say, 'the being is in movement,' is determined by the category of the πρός τι, the 'being-in-relation-to-an-other,' namely, the moving thing characterized by ποίησις, the moved thing by πάθησις" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 232). Accordingly, movement is always relational—it involves an active and a passive pole, a mover and a moved—and in the case of animal locomotion these poles are internalized within the living being itself, which is at once the source and the subject of its own movement. Furthermore, Heidegger draws attention to the connection between ἐνέργεια and κίνησις, noting that "ἐνέργεια, specifically, is related in itself πρὸς τὴν ἐντελέχειαν" and that historically the name ἐνέργεια "came to be carried over to the other, to what contrasted with determinations of movement" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 213–215). This the relationship between movement and actuality is not one of simple identity but of complex analogy: movement is a kind of incomplete actuality, an ἐνέργεια ἀτελής, while the full realization of a capacity is ἐντελέχεια in the strict sense. It is perhaps this incompleteness that gives animal movement its characteristic temporal extension—its quality of being-on-the-way toward an end that has not yet been achieved. Thus the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit, far from being a merely mechanical sequence, constitutes a richly structured ontological and psychological phenomenon: phantasia discloses the object under a motivationally salient description; orexis reaches toward or recoils from the object so disclosed; and kinesis actualizes the living being's potentiality for locomotion in response to the conjunction of appearance and desire. The circuit operates at every level of animal life, from the sensitive phantasia of non-rational animals to the deliberative phantasia of rational agents; and it is precisely through this circuit that the living being is able to navigate the virtual world of practically significant appearances that constitutes its environment. The investigation of this circuit in De Anima III.9–11 and De Motu Animalium 6–8 thus reveals the deep integration of Aristotle's psychology with his physics and his ontology of movement, and it establishes phantasia—however difficult it may be to translate—as the indispensable mediating term between perception, desire, and the locomotive activity that defines animal life as such. --- # VALIDATION APPENDIX ## Claim Map | # | Claim | Source | Page(s) |
